 CORE

Highlight

FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors associated with Dupuytren disease.
Review the anatomy of pathologic fascial cords.
Describe the classic appearance of Dupuytren disease and the common contractures the
cords create.
Describe the surgical and nonsurgical management of Dupuytren disease.
Compare the advantages, risks, adverse effects, and cost implications associated with the
three primary treatment options for Dupuytren disease: needle aponeurotomy, collagenase
injection, and surgical management (fasciectomy versus partial fasciectomy).
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview and Definition




NOTES

Characterized by abnormal thickening of the palmar fascia
Thickened fascia creates cords and/or nodules in the hand and palm.
Cords lead to fascial contracture with eventual joint and digit contractures.
Pathologic fibroblasts and myofibroblasts are the culprit.

Overview and Definition
Dupuytren disease is a nodular thickening and contraction of the palmar fascia beneath
the skin (Figure 1; Resource 1). Thickened fascia features high concentrations of
fibroblasts and contractile myofibroblasts, resulting in eventual fascial contracture. The
disease may be referred to as Dupuytren disease, Dupuytren contracture, Palmar
fibromatosis, or Viking disease.
Figure 1 Images show Dupuytren disease of the ring finger. A, Illustration of a hand
shows the affected palmar fascial cord. Palmar (B) and lateral (C) view clinical
photographs of the hands of a patient with bilateral Dupuytren disease. The ring finger
of the right hand, the little finger of the left hand, and both palms are affected. (Panel A
adapted with permission from the American Society for Surgery of the Hand: Dupuytren’s
Disease. Englewood, CO, 1995. Panels B and C reproduced from Adams JE: Dupuytren
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
2/25

contracture, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 474-476.)
The disease also may affect the soles of the feet (Lederhosen disease), the dorsal aspect
of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP joints; knuckle pads or Garrod pads), or the penis in
males (Peyronie disease). Involvement in multiple areas is known as Dupuytren diathesis
and is believed to be associated with a more progressive disease course (Figure 1).
Epidemiology
Males of Northern European descent are most affected.
Increasing prevalence of Dupuytren disease with increasing age
Genetics usually are autosomal dominant with an incomplete penetrance inheritance pattern;
however, other modes of genetic transmission and nongenetic disease are possible.1
Comorbidity risks incompletely understood
Dupuytren disease most commonly affects men older than 50 years.

Epidemiology
Dupuytren disease is noted to have an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with
incomplete penetrance in most genetic studies. Individuals may have the gene and pass
it on without any manifestations of the disease occurring. Other genetic and nongenetic
disease is possible. Dupuytren disease most commonly affects men older than 50 years.1
Males appear to have a higher incidence of contractures, which may be related to
identification of testosterone receptors in the palmar fascia; however, women may have
a high risk of palmar fascial thickening without contractures. In a review of new patients
presenting to a hand specialist over a 16-month period, 37% had palmar fibromatosis
(33% men and 40% women); increasing prevalence with age was noted. Only 8% of these
patients had contractures, and of those with contractures, only one in five presented for
management of the contracture.2 women or younger patients who exhibit disease and
those in whom the disease rapidly progresses may be at risk for worse disease; however,
whether this can be supported by experimental evidence remains unclear.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
3/25

Some speculate that Dupuytren disease may be associated with diabetes mellitus, anti-
seizure medications, alcohol use, tobacco use, hypercholesterolemia, liver disease, HIV,
adhesive capsulitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and specific activities, all of which may be
associated with a correlation rather than causation, with possible confounding factors.
High-quality experimental evidence is lacking to support these associations. Diabetic
Cheiroarthropathy (skin thickening and joint stiffness in the setting of diabetes mellitus)
may exist concomitantly or be confused with Dupuytren disease.
An association of palmar fascial thickening after fracture or surgery of the hand or wrist
also is noted. Long-standing mild disease rather than a new pathology may be noticed
after these events. It can also be theorized that trauma may be associated with
increased Dupuytren changes in the hand.
Natural History

Natural History
No factors are associated with the rate and degree of contracture progression, other
than past performance is indicative of the future. Meaning that patients who experience
rapid onset and changes in the hand may continue to have a similar rate of findings,
while those with slow and indolent progress are more likely to have a future
characterized by similar indolent course. Pain is uncommon and generally self-limiting.
Milesi3 reported on his observations of 150 untreated patients with thickening and no
contracture seeking hand management, noting that some degree of contracture
occurred within 3 to 5 years in 37% of the hands and within 6 to 12 years in 46% of the
hands. Given the number of individuals seeking a hand specialist for Dupuytren disease
with minimal or no contracture, this estimate appears to be somewhat high and may
include patients with very limited contracture. More data are necessary on the natural
history of Dupuytren disease.
Basic Science
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
4/25

The diseased tissue originates in longitudinally oriented, normal fascial structures.
Characterized by three phases: early proliferative, involutional, and residual
Fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblast is associated with contracture.
Type III collagen and several growth factors implicated

Basic Science
The early proliferative phase is characterized by high cell concentrations of immature
fibroblasts and myofibroblasts in a whorled pattern; this early hypercellular structure
often is referred to as a histologic nodule.
In the involutional phase, fibroblasts align along tension lines and produce more
collagen. The final residual phase is relatively acellular and features contracted, collagen-
laden tissue more characteristic of scar formation.
The myofibroblast is the cellular contractile culprit of Dupuytren disease. The
myofibroblast differs from the fibroblast in that it has actual bundles of contractile actin
microfilaments arranged parallel to the long axis of the cell. Adjacent myofibroblasts
connect via extracellular fibrils of fibronectin and act together to generate the contracted
tissue observed in patients with Dupuytren disease. Increasing levels of mechanical
tension also have been shown to influence fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblasts.
Type III collagen is more prevalent in the extracellular matrix in patients with Dupuytren
disease. Transforming growth factor-beta 1, transforming growth factor-beta 2,
epidermal growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor, and connective tissue growth
factor all have been suggested to play a role in initiating abnormal cellular proliferation.
Normal Palmar Anatomy
Natatory ligament
Grayson and Cleland ligaments
Fibers/pretendinous bands (Figure 2; Resource 2)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
5/25

Figure 2 Illustration shows the normal fascial anatomy of the palm and digits, revealing
relationships of the fascia to the tendon sheath and the neurovascular bundles. (Reproduced
from Blazer PE: Dupuytren contracture, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 331-336.)
Lateral digital sheet—Running lateral to and alongside the neurovascular bundles, the lateral
digital sheet is formed by merging fibers of the spiral band and natatory ligament.

Normal Palmar Anatomy
This transverse structure resides just under the skin at each commissure, sending fibers
distally along the lateral border of each digit to merge with the lateral digital sheet.
These ligaments maintain digital skin position relative to deeper structures. The Grayson
ligament is palmar to the neurovascular bundle and passes from the flexor sheath to the
skin. The Cleland ligament is dorsal to the bundle and arises from the phalanges. The
Cleland ligament is relatively uninvolved in Dupuytren disease. The Grayson ligament
may become part of a lateral cord if it joins the diseased lateral digital sheet. SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
6/25

In the proximal palm, fibers of the palmar fascia are contiguous with the palmaris longus
or the deep fascia of the forearm and continue distally toward the digits as pretendinous
bands; each band lies superficial to the corresponding flexor tendon sheath for that
digit.
At the level of the distal palmar crease (DPC), transverse fibers of the palmar fascia run
just dorsal to the pretendinous bands and are not involved in the contractile process
observed in patients with Dupuytren disease; the disease affects structures along
longitudinal lines of tension. The location of these transverse, normal fascial bands is
important surgically because the neurovascular bundles are consistently dorsal or deep
to these bands, facilitating identification of the bundles in the palm.
Beyond the DPC, the pretendinous band fibers divide into three layers, along which the
disease process also follows (Table 1).
Table 1
Layers of the Pretendinous Band Fibers
Layer
Characteristics
1
The pretendinous band sends off skin attachment fibers between the distal
palmar crease and the metacarpophalangeal joint crease; if these fibers
become diseased, nodules and skin pits form at this level.
2
Spiral bands emerge from either side of the pretendinous band and pass
distally along either side of the flexor sheath, passing under the
neurovascular bundle (this relationship becomes important if the spiral
band becomes involved in the contracture) to merge with the lateral digital
sheet.
3
Flimsy perforating fibers from the pretendinous band pass dorsally around
either side of the metacarpophalangeal joint, merging with the extensor
tendons.
Based on data from Blazar PE: Dupuytren contracture, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 331-336.
Pathologic Anatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
7/25

Bands and cords—Normal anatomic structures are called bands; diseased or contracted
structures are referred to as cords (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustration of a finger shows patterns of diseased cords. The spiral cord (derived
from the pretendinous band, spiral band, Grayson ligament, and lateral digital sheet) displaces
the neurovascular bundle toward the midline. The Grayson ligament is observed as an isolated
thickened structure. The lateral cord comes off the natatory cord to merge with the lateral
digital sheet along the midaxial line. (Reproduced from Blazer PE: Dupuytren contracture, in
Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 331-336.)
Central cord generally leads to metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint contracture
Spiral cord generally leads to PIP joint contracture.
Natatory cord results in web space contracture.
Retrovascular cord (Figure 4) leads to distal interphalangeal joint contracture.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
8/25

Figure 4 Illustration of a finger shows the retrovascular cord, which arises from the preaxial
phalanx and courses dorsal to the neurovascular bundle to insert in the side of the distal
phalanx. The retrovascular cord is the usual cause of distal interphalangeal joint
contractures. (Reproduced from Blazer PE: Dupuytren contracture, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 331-336.)
Nodules

Pathologic Anatomy
The central cord results from disease involvement of the pretendinous bands. Palmar
nodules and pits form beyond the DPC. Fibers from the cord extend and insert along the
flexor sheath around the PIP joint level; this usually results in MCP joint contracture. The
central cord is not involved with the neurovascular bundle.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
9/25

The spiral cord results from contracture of the spiral bands that pass dorsal to the
neurovascular bundle to merge with the lateral digital sheet and the Grayson ligament;
this generally results in contracture of the PIP joint.
The term spiral cord may be a misnomer because the structure actually becomes
thickened and straight as it becomes diseased; as this occurs, it displaces the
neurovascular bundle superficially, proximally, and toward the midline, rendering the
bundle vulnerable to injury during disease resection.
The components forming the spiral cord are the pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral
digital sheet, and Grayson ligament.
The natatory cord develops from the distal fibers of the natatory ligament, just under the
commissure skin. It results in a web space contracture.
The retrovascular cord can arise dorsal to the neurovascular bundle, taking origin from
the proximal phalanx and inserting onto the distal phalanx. It is the usual cause of a
distal interphalangeal joint contracture.
Nodules often appear before actual contractile cords and do not always progress to
cords during a patient’s lifetime. They can be found in the palm but also may occur
dorsally over the PIP joint, called Garrod papules.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients may initially notice one or more painless nodule near the DPC.
Occasionally, they may be slightly tender but most are painless.
The ring finger is most commonly involved, followed by the little finger, the long finger, the
thumb, and the index finger.
Finger flexion is normal.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
10/25

Patients with notable contractures may report trouble grasping objects, pulling on gloves, and
putting the hand into a pocket.
Physical Examination
Palmar subcutaneous nodule that may resemble a callus
Abnormal cords extend distally and occasionally proximally from the nodule.
These bands may cross the PIP joint and commonly cross the MCP joint, limiting finger
extension.
The bands are seldom tender, except for some patients in the preliminary stages of the
disease.
Diagnostic Tests
Diagnosis is made based on clinical examination.
No imaging studies or other diagnostic tests are performed.
Ultrasonography or MRI may be ordered by a non-specialist unfamiliar with the disease or if
the diagnosis is in question; however advanced imaging studies usually are not helpful and will
reveal thickened tissue with a nonspecific appearance.
Neurovascular Examination
Identify any nerve dysfunction from other disease (eg, median neuropathy at the carpal
tunnel) or prior injury.
Differential Diagnosis
Flexion contracture secondary to joint or tendon injury (no cords or bands)
Locked trigger finger (no associated nodules). Flexion at distal interphalangeal joint. Opens
with anesthesia and manipulation.
Posturing from neurologic pathology or clenched fist syndrome (no cords, bands, or nodules)
Diabetic Cheiroarthropathy Skin and joint stiffness associated with diabetes mellitus
Management
Nonsurgical/Nonprocedural Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
11/25

No nonsurgical treatment options have been experimentally proven to alter the natural history
of the disease. Splints, corticosteroid injections, and radiation therapy are described but
inadequately tested.
The primary treatment option is information, correction of common misconceptions, and
reassurance.
Radiation Therapy

Radiation Therapy
Occasionally, radiation therapy is used as an adjunct in the management of benign
proliferative conditions characterized by increased cellular activity, such as in keloid
scars or heterotopic ossification. In Dupuytren disease, low-dose irradiation may inhibit
fibroblast proliferation via the nitric oxide synthetase pathway.4 Typically, a low dosage
of 30 Gy is used. A recent systematic review concluded that radiation therapy should be
considered an unproven treatment option because of scarce evidence and unknown
long-term adverse effects.4
Corticosteroid Injection

Corticosteroid Injection
The rationale for steroid injection is that Dupuytren disease is a localized inflammatory
disorder. Steroid use, including intralesional injection, topical, intramuscular, or oral
applications, has been reported. A recent systematic review showed no benefit to
systemic steroids and limited data on the efficacy of topical steroids. Intralesional
injection studies showed improvement in non-standardized reports from patients or
surgeons with few adverse events; however, the studies had severe limitations.
Experimental evidence is lacking.5
Procedural Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
12/25

Procedures that may be considered:
Collagenase injection to the involved cord
Percutaneous aponeurotomy using a needle to rupture cords.
Surgery to excise or incise the thick cords, release of the joint contractures, which may
include leaving the skin to heal via secondary intent versus skin closure
Procedures are considered in patients with a 30° fixed flexion deformity of the MCP joint or a
10° deformity of the PIP joint.

Procedural Management
More severe contractures, particularly at the PIP joint, are more difficult to correct,
associated with a higher incidence of recurrent contracture, and often are accompanied
by a longer course of postoperative therapy. Whether this should be used as a
justification for earlier management given the unpredictable natural history of the
disease remains unclear.
Collagenase (Resources 3 and 4)
Collagenase isolated from Clostridium histolyticum can be injected to pathologic cords.
Collagenase contains a metalloprotease enzyme that binds to and lyses the three-dimensional
structure of collagen.
Has extremely low activity against type IV collagen (the main basement membrane collagen
component of nerves and blood vessels), which explains the low neurovascular complication
rate observed
Injection is followed by stretch manipulation 24 hours to several days after injection to rupture
the cord. This is then typically followed by a splinting and stretching protocol to manage
residual joint contracture.
Self-limiting adverse events, such as peripheral edema, bruising, skin tear, pain, or temporary
lymphadenopathy, are common (approximately 94%) after collagenase management.6 Major
complications, including flexor tendon ruptures, pulley ruptures, and anaphylaxis, occur in less
than 1% of patients.
Recurrence rates higher than those with surgical release
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
13/25

The current best available data report an overall 5-year recurrence rate of 39% for MCP joint
contractures and 66% for PIP joint contractures.7
The costs associated with collagenase typically are higher than those with other nonsurgical
treatment options. Published cost estimates are approximately $4,000 to $5,000 per injection,
which currently typically are covered by many insurance plans.
Needle Aponeurotomy (Resource 5; Video 1)
Percutaneous needle aponeurotomy is a method of dividing contracted cords without an
incision.
The procedure is performed with the use of local anesthesia to numb the skin only, generally
in the office setting, followed by gradual division of the cord via multiple needle punctures.
Aponeurotomy offers immediate reduction of contracture and affords the greatest
improvement in MCP joints compared with PIP joints.
Contracture improvement after aponeurotomy is less than that observed after open partial
fasciectomy, with a higher recurrence rate. The 5-year recurrence rate is higher than 85%.
Needle aponeurotomy may be a better treatment option than surgical treatment in patients
with milder contractures and medical comorbidities that place them at surgical risk. In general,
the post-procedure rehabilitation is less burdensome than that after surgical management or
collagenase injections.
The estimated cost per digit is approximately $600, making it the cheapest procedural
treatment option.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
14/25

Video 1 Villanueva M, Fahandez-Saddi H, Iborra A Sr: Ultrasonographic-Guided Aponeurotomy
For Dupuytren Contracture [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/21552__Videos. Accessed April 27, 2021.
Multiple scant injections of local anesthesia are performed over the cord, ideally to anesthetize
the skin only and not the digital nerves. Subsequently, the surgeon palpates the cord and uses
a needle to percutaneously divide the cord. This is followed by manipulation to fully release
the diseased cord and manipulation of any residual joint contractures. This typically is followed
by a splinting and stretching protocol to relieve residual joint contracture. Most patients are
instructed to wear a nighttime splint in extension for 6 weeks.
Surgical Management
(Videos 2 and 3)
Techniques/Procedures
Palmar fasciectomy (Resource 6)
Limited fasciectomy involves removal of all diseased tissue in a ray (or rays) via dissection,
generally proceeding in a proximal to distal direction; despite the term limited, accomplishing
this may require a great deal of dissection in a given ray.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
15/25

Radical fasciectomy involves the release of all palmar and digital fascia, even that which does
not appear to be diseased. This procedure is performed infrequently because of its higher
complication rates and minimal effect on recurrence.
Video 2 Karbach LE, Hammert WC, Schreck M: Limited Palmar and Digital Dermofasciectomy for
Management of Recurrent Dupuytren Disease [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2019.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/20236__Videos. Accessed April 27, 2021.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
16/25

Video 3 Julka A, Roebke AJ, Seaman AP: Dupuytren Contracture: Technique for Spiral Cord
Fasciectomy [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/21595__Videos. Accessed April 27, 2021.
Patient Positioning
The patient typically is placed in the supine position with the hand outstretched on a hand
table.
Appropriate equipment is required, including access to micro-instrumentation in the rare
instance that digit ischemia occurs.
Historically, patients underwent anesthesia with tourniquet use for visualization; however, the
advent of wide-awake local anesthesia without a tourniquet surgery is pushing the boundaries
of hand surgery, and some surgeons use this technique for the management of Dupuytren
disease.
Surgical Approaches
Various skin incisions can be used. The incision should be individualized for the patient based
on the location of the diseased tissue, the presence of recurrent disease with prior incisions or
diseased skin, and the need for potential lengthening of skin.
Brunner zigzag incisions, multiple V-Y incisions, sequential Z-plasty, or skin grafts can be used
to lengthen skin. Video 4 shows the typical Brunner incisions to expose the palmar structures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
17/25

Dermofasciectomy (excision of overlying skin with diseased fascia), arthrodesis, or amputation
may be required in patients with recurrent or advanced disease. In patients with recurrent
disease and skin involvement, resection of the skin with subsequent full-thickness skin grafting
frequently is performed.
The open-palm technique (McCash technique), which involves leaving a transverse skin incision
open at the level of the DPC, avoids postoperative hematoma formation and may help
minimize stiffness during recovery
PIP joint contracture with a nodule or tuft of diseased tissue just beyond the MCP joint should
alert the surgeon to the strong possibility of a spiral cord with midline superficial and proximal
displacement of the digital nerve.
Video 4 Uhl RL: Volar approach to the finger using the Brunner incision: Extensive exposure,
in Uhl RL, ed: Selective Exposures in Orthopaedic Surgery: The Hand [DVD]. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2006.
This method has been shown to result in longer healing time and greater recurrence than
coverage of the palmar defect via local transposition of a radially based flap with full-thickness
skin graft coverage of the resulting donor site.
Postoperative Management
Typically, a volar resting splint keeping the joints in maximal extension
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
18/25

Close follow-up to monitor any tenuous skin flaps and given the relatively higher rates of
postoperative complications compared with most elective hand surgery
Referral to physical therapy is common for custom-molded extension splinting, edema control,
range of motion, and wound care.
Typically, patients experience difficulty and stiffness in flexion and extension postoperatively.
After the first 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively, during which active, active assisted, and passive
motion is encouraged at home and in a supervised fashion, patients generally are transitioned
to nighttime extension splint use for 3 to 6 months postoperatively.
Complications
Patients may experience nerve injury, skin loss, and recurrence of the disease postoperatively
or after management. Complications range from mild adverse events to major limb-
threatening complications.
Digital Ischemia
Digital ischemia may result from iatrogenic arterial transection or vessel traction injury in the
form of spasm, intimal hemorrhage, or actual rupture. This may occur after surgical release
and nonsurgical management (collagenase, needle aponeurotomy).
Ischemia usually results from correction of long-standing joint contracture, with associated
vessels having inadequate elasticity.
Digital artery injury has been reported in 2% of patients who undergo surgical fasciectomy
(range, 0% to 2.6%).8
The surgeon should allow the joint to return to a relaxed posture and warm the patient and
the digit.
Topical lidocaine or papaverine or calcium channel blocker administration also can be
attempted to help relieve vasospasm.
Recalcitrant vasospasm may require leaving the digit in a flexed posture to relieve traction on
the digital arteries.
If a thrombosed segment of vessel is identified in an ischemic digit, an interpositional vein
graft may be necessary.
Nerve Injury
Neurapraxia is not uncommon in the management of the disease.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
19/25

Nerve dysfunction usually is ascribed to handling and protection intraoperatively and also may
be related to long-standing contracture and traction neuropathy on digit extension.
A recent systematic review found rates of neurapraxia variable among treatment options.
Rate of injury was 0 to 52% for fasciectomy, 2% to 3% for aponeurotomy, and not reported
for collagenase.8
Symptoms usually are self-limiting and do not require management. Complete loss of
sensibility that persists more than 3 months without signs of improvement may suggest
laceration and may warrant exploration and repair.
Iatrogenic partial or complete nerve transection identified intraoperatively is repaired
primarily.
Intraoperatively, the risk of nerve or vessel injury in patients with recurrent disease is fivefold
and tenfold higher, respectively, compared with primary disease.
A spiral cord displaces the digital nerve to a superficial midline and proximal position, placing it
at risk for transection.
Management of nerve laceration is immediate primary neurorrhaphy.
Wound Complications
Wound separation, wound edge necrosis, and larger areas of devascularized skin flaps
frequently occur.
Skin tears or defects also are common.
Most wound complications heal uneventfully with dressing changes.
Infection
Infection usually is superficial and can be managed via oral antibiotic agents. Deep infection is
relatively uncommon.
Patients with peripheral vascular disease or diabetes mellitus have a higher risk for prolonged
wound healing and infection.
Postoperative Swelling and Hematoma
Postoperative swelling and hematoma contribute to prolonged stiffness and early wound-
healing difficulties, particularly in patients who undergo surgical treatment.
Early reduction of edema is a key aspect of postoperative recovery and is best achieved by
active movement and use of the hand.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:01 PM
AAOS | Dupuytren Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004032
20/25

Tourniquet deflation is performed and careful hemostasis measurements should be obtained
before closure.
Collagenase and Aponeurotomy Complications
Similar to surgical complications, complications occur in patients who undergo needle
aponeurotomy and collagenase.
Unique to collagenase is the risk of anaphylactic reaction to the medication.
The other major risk is tendon rupture. Rates of both of these complications are less than 1%.6
Soft-tissue reactions, including swelling, hematoma, bruising, peripheral edema, contusion,
and pain, are almost universal with collagenase because of the reaction of the enzyme.
A systematic review reported rates of at least one treatment-related adverse event to be 94%
with collagenase.6
Outcomes
Recurrence
Recurrence of the contracture is always possible.
Early age, Dupuytren diathesis, multifocal disease, PIP joint disease, and small finger
contracture may have some predictive value in identifying patients at risk for recurrence.
Recurrence of Dupuytren disease is approximately 30% during postoperative years one and
two, 15% during postoperative years three through five, 10% during postoperative years five
through 10, and less than 10% after 10 years postoperatively.
Comparative Results
At this time, several randomized trials are ongoing or beginning to compare treatment
techniques; however, current results are not conclusive in favoring one treatment option over
another.
Recent comparative studies have focused on four key factors of management: complications,
advantages, costs, and recurrence.
Major complications include tendon or pulley rupture, nerve damage, or ischemia. These are
rare among all the treatment options (<1%). Minor complications, also called adverse events in
the literature, are highest with collagenase at 93%. Anaphylaxis is unique to collagenase
medication.

Advantages of surgical fasciectomy are the lowest risk of recurrence and the highest rate of
contracture correction compared with collagenase and aponeurotomy. Advantages of
nonsurgical treatment options are the avoidance of surgical incisions and postoperative
healing.
Collagenase and aponeurotomy have a lower cost compared with surgical management, with
aponeurotomy being the cheapest treatment option; however, a recent study by Leafblad et
al9 showed that, although surgical management was associated with the highest initial cost, if
accounting for reintervention, the cumulative cost was similar to that of collagenase and was
associated with the lowest reintervention rate.
Recurrence rates are lowest in patients who undergo surgical fasciectomy and highest in
patients who undergo collagenase or aponeurotomy. Collagenase and aponeurotomy are
associated with similar correction and recurrence rates at 2- and 5-year follow-up. Recurrence
among all treatment types is higher in PIP joints than MCP joints.
Summary
Patients can be informed that Dupuytren disease cannot be cured and always is associated
with a risk for recurrence or progression.
Nodules or cords that do not result in contracture and do not impair function are observed
and may or may not result in contracture.
Treatment has traditionally been considered in patients with a flexion contracture of 30° at the
MCP joint or more than 0° at the PIP joint; however, treatment is always discretionary, allowing
the patient to decide, with careful correction of common misconceptions.
Recurrence by joint is higher in PIP joint than MCP joint contractures.
Although fasciectomy remains the preferred treatment option, the low rates of recurrence can
be weighed against morbidity and recovery time.8
Less invasive treatment options, such as needle aponeurotomy or collagenase injection, are
increasingly popular.
Comparative studies are ongoing; however, several early generalizations may be deduced.
Recurrence is highest in patients who undergo collagenase and lowest in patients who
undergo surgical fasciectomy.
Cost is lowest with aponeurotomy followed by collagenase and highest with surgical
management; however, cumulative cost models accounting for recurrence make surgical
management cheaper than collagenase.
